variants.name: String-literal union with as const source of truth
variants.idiom_name: as const object + derived literal union type
variants.implementation_notes: The modern TypeScript realization is type-level: a union of string literals closes the set at compile time, and an `as const` object provides the runtime values so there is one source of truth. Nothing is emitted for the type, callers may use raw literals, and runtime validation uses the object's values. The TypeScript handbook itself notes that an object with as const may replace an enum; this variant is the default for new code.
pitfalls: The union is erased: `raw as Suit` or an unvalidated JSON string bypasses it, so every external value needs the parse function.
A bare union duplicated at several sites drifts; keep the as-const object as the single source of truth and derive the type from it.
Literal unions do not give a nominal type: any string typed as Suit is still a string, so overloads and branded types are needed if true nominality is required.

variants.name: TypeScript enum keyword (string-initialised)
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript's enum construct is nominally typed: a raw string is not assignable to the enum type, so it delivers the pattern's separation directly, and string members serialize readably. Use it when you explicitly want enum semantics or are interoperating with code that does; initialise every member with a string, because numeric members accept any number and add reverse mappings. Avoid const enum in published code - it is incompatible with isolatedModules, Babel and type-stripping runtimes.
pitfalls: Numeric enums accept any number ((Suit)99 compiles) and add reverse mapping objects; always use string members.
const enum inlines values at compile time and breaks under isolatedModules, Babel, SWC or Node's type stripping (the handbook's own pitfall list).
Enum members cannot be used as bare literals in APIs that accept strings without an explicit conversion, which often forces casts at boundaries.
